title: A New Light-Powered Material Makes Hydrogen From Water
summary:
Chemists at Oregon State University have found a new way to make hydrogen from water using light. The work was led by Kyriakos Stylianou of the university's College of Science. His team developed a material called a photocatalyst that can produce hydrogen quickly and efficiently.

Hydrogen is used in fuel cells for vehicles. It is also used to make ammonia, refine metals and manufacture plastics.

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being permanently changed. A photocatalyst is similar, but light switches it on. After it absorbs light, it reaches a higher energy state and can use that energy to drive reactions faster. The results were published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. Stylianou said they could give researchers another tool for reducing greenhouse gases.

The team studies metal organic frameworks, or MOFs. These are crystal-like materials full of tiny pores, built from metal ions and organic molecules called linkers. Scientists have already made nearly 100,000 different MOFs. This study focused on one called BVR-19. It has an unusual sulfur-to-sulfur bond that briefly breaks in light, creating very reactive sulfur pieces. Stylianou said the material's sulfur-containing building blocks capture light energy and move electrons, so it does not need an extra expensive metal catalyst. It also forms on its own in water at room temperature.

Most hydrogen today is made from natural gas, a process that releases carbon dioxide. It costs about $1.50 per kilogram, while "green" hydrogen costs roughly $5 per kilogram. Stylianou said the work gives new design rules for making materials that could bring down the cost of green hydrogen.
why_it_matters: Making hydrogen more cheaply without releasing carbon dioxide could give researchers another tool for cutting greenhouse gases.
